lessonTitle: Chronic Disease Management in Primary Care: Review, Targets and Medicines Optimisation

blocks.text: Mrs Okafor, 61, has attended the practice diabetes clinic every year for a decade. Asked what her last HbA1c was and what it should be, she shrugs: 'The nurse knows.' Her numbers have never been hers, and her control has drifted. Long-term care that is done to a patient, rather than with them, is the central failure that structured chronic disease management tries to fix.

blocks.markdown:
**Structured review.** In UK general practice, most long-term care is delivered through *recall systems*: a register of patients with a condition (for example type 2 diabetes, hypertension or asthma), an invitation at least annually, a protocol-driven review, and a record that makes the next review safer. The Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) rewards practices for delivering many of these processes and outcomes; it is a population-level incentive scheme, not an individual patient's treatment plan. Check the current QOF indicator set, because it changes each year.

A good review has three parts: **(1)** measure (for example weight, blood pressure, HbA1c, peak flow or symptom control, inhaler technique); **(2)** screen for complications and comorbidity (feet, eyes and kidneys in diabetes; cardiovascular risk in hypertension; exacerbations and reliever overuse in asthma); **(3)** agree actions and a follow-up plan with the patient.

blocks.title: Self-management support
blocks.text: Self-management support is the set of education, skills training and tools that enable a patient to manage their own condition day to day: understanding the condition, monitoring (for example home blood pressure or a symptom diary), recognising deterioration, and following a written personalised action plan that says what to do and when to seek help. It is a partnership, not a hand-over of responsibility.

rows: HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids and cardiovascular risk, kidney function (eGFR and urine albumin:creatinine ratio), foot check, retinal screening status, weight, medicines review
Structured education, home or clinic glucose monitoring where indicated, foot care advice, hypoglycaemia recognition if on relevant drugs
Clinic blood pressure, cardiovascular risk assessment, renal function, adherence and adverse effects, lifestyle
Home blood pressure monitoring with a validated device, salt and alcohol advice, diary of readings
Symptom control (for example a validated questionnaire), reliever use, exacerbations and oral steroid courses, inhaler technique, smoking status
Written personalised asthma action plan, peak flow or symptom diary, trigger avoidance, knowing when to seek urgent help
blocks.caption: Review content is a teaching summary; check current NICE and local guidance for the full protocol.

blocks.markdown:
**Individual treatment targets.** A target is a number or goal that the patient and clinician agree is worth pursuing for *this* person. Guidelines give a default range, but the right target depends on the patient's age, frailty, life expectancy, comorbidity, risk of harm from treatment (particularly hypoglycaemia or postural hypotension), and what matters to them. For example, a tighter HbA1c target may suit a younger person on lifestyle measures alone, while a more relaxed target is often appropriate for a frail older person on a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia. For blood pressure, home or ambulatory readings run lower than clinic readings, so the target must state which measurement method it refers to. Check current NICE guidance (NG28 diabetes, NG136 hypertension, and the asthma guidance) for the default values rather than memorising a single number.

HbA1c is reported in IFCC units (mmol/mol), with the older DCCT percentage still seen in some papers and by some patients. The two are related linearly:

blocks.caption: IFCC to DCCT conversion; the inverse is mmol/mol = (% - 2.15) / 0.0915

blocks.title: Converting a percentage HbA1c to mmol/mol
blocks.prompt: A patient's old hospital letter says her HbA1c was 7.5%. Express this in mmol/mol and say what to tell her about reading the new report.

steps.text: Write the conversion in inverse form, because we start from the percentage.
Divide: 5.35 divided by 0.0915 is about 58.5, so the value is approximately 58 mmol/mol (laboratories report whole numbers, so 58 or 59 depending on rounding of the original percentage).
Explain to the patient that new reports use mmol/mol, that a *lower* number means better control in both systems, and that her target is a number agreed with her, not a generic one.

blocks.answer: About 58 mmol/mol. Both scales fall as control improves, so it is vital that the patient and the team quote the same units.

blocks.title: Targets belong to the patient
blocks.text: A shared target is individualised, recorded in the notes, reviewed regularly and revised when circumstances change (new frailty, a hypoglycaemic episode, pregnancy planning). The question is not 'what does the guideline say' alone but 'what is right for this patient given the benefits and harms of treatment'.

blocks.markdown: **The primary care team.** Long-term conditions are rarely managed by a GP alone. The *GP* provides diagnosis, complexity management and prescribing oversight. The *practice nurse* or specialist nurse often runs the structured clinic, measures, teaches and titrates medicines under agreed protocols. *Healthcare assistants* take routine measurements and recall. The *practice or clinical pharmacist* undertakes structured medication reviews and addresses polypharmacy. *Community pharmacists* support correct use of new medicines and inhaler technique. Other contributors include dietitians, podiatrists, health coaches, social prescribers and secondary care specialists for complex cases.

headers: Typical contribution to long-term condition care
rows: Diagnosis, complex multimorbidity, prescribing oversight, safety-netting, coordination
Structured review clinics, education, inhaler technique, monitoring, protocol-led titration
Measurements (weight, BP, foot checks where trained), recall, simple health coaching
Structured medication review, deprescribing, polypharmacy, medicines reconciliation after discharge
Dispensing, new medicine support, inhaler technique, adherence conversations
blocks.caption: Roles overlap and vary between practices; scope of practice is set locally and by professional regulation.

blocks.markdown: **Medicines optimisation.** NICE describes medicines optimisation (NG5) as ensuring that the right patients get the right choice of medicine, at the right time, with a focus on outcomes. Its four guiding principles are: understand the patient's experience; make an evidence-based choice of medicines; ensure that medicines use is as safe as possible; and make medicines optimisation part of routine practice. In practice this means asking what the patient actually takes, checking whether it is still needed (deprescribing), and looking at adherence. A useful, objective adherence proxy from repeat-prescription data is the *proportion of days covered*.

blocks.latex: \text{PDC} = \dfrac{\text{days' supply collected in the interval}}{\text{days in the interval}} \times 100\%
blocks.caption: PDC: proportion of days covered. Low PDC suggests under-use but does not tell you why.

blocks.title: Interpreting a refill record
blocks.prompt: A patient was prescribed a once-daily tablet in 28-day packs. Over a 112-day interval she collected 3 packs. Estimate the proportion of days covered and say how you would use it.

steps.text: Total days' supply collected: 3 packs of 28 days each.
Divide by the length of the interval, 112 days.
Convert to a percentage: PDC is 75%, meaning one day in four had no tablet available according to the record.

Use this as the start of a non-judgemental conversation: ask about side effects, beliefs and practical barriers, rather than concluding that she is non-adherent. Stockpiles or supplies from elsewhere could explain a low figure.

blocks.answer: PDC = 75%. It is a prompt for a conversation, not a diagnosis of non-adherence.

blocks.title: Agreeing a blood pressure approach together
blocks.prompt: A 72-year-old man with hypertension has clinic readings above his target but says home readings are lower. Walk through how you would agree a plan.

steps.text: Ask about his ideas, concerns and expectations, including worry about tablets or dizziness, before presenting numbers.

Offer home blood pressure monitoring with a validated device, with teaching on technique and on how many readings to take (check current NICE advice on the protocol); ask him to bring the diary or device.
Compare home readings with the home target (which differs from the clinic target), recording the method with the target in the notes.

Agree who will do what: his role (taking readings, reporting dizziness), the nurse's role (review in a set interval) and the pharmacist's role (medication review), and put the review date in the record.

blocks.answer: Plan agreed jointly, based on home readings against a home target, with named roles and a review date.

points: Structured review (recall system, measure, screen, agree actions) and self-management support (education, monitoring, written action plans) are the backbone of long-term care.
Targets are agreed with the patient, individualised to age, frailty, risk of harm and preferences, and must state the measurement method; check current NICE guidance for defaults.
Care is delivered by a team: nurses, healthcare assistants, pharmacists and GPs, each with defined roles.
Medicines optimisation puts the patient's experience first, aims for safe and effective use, and uses tools such as structured medication review and adherence data without blaming the patient.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a personalised asthma action plan?

options.text: A hospital discharge letter that records the dose of oral steroids given
A generic leaflet about asthma that is the same for every patient
A written, individualised plan that tells the patient how to recognise worsening control and what to do at each stage, including when to seek urgent help
A list of the patient's repeat medicines kept in the practice computer system

questions.correctOptionText: A written, individualised plan that tells the patient how to recognise worsening control and what to do at each stage, including when to seek urgent help

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: a discharge letter records a past event rather than guiding self-management.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: generic information is not personalised and does not state individual triggers or actions.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it is personalised, written and action-oriented.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a medicines list is not an action plan and does not guide the patient in worsening symptoms.

questions.explanation: A personalised action plan is the core self-management tool in asthma because it empowers the patient to act early and recognise when professional help is needed. Generic leaflets and medicines lists inform but do not tell the patient what to do as symptoms change.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old frail woman with type 2 diabetes takes a sulfonylurea, has had two hypoglycaemic episodes this winter, and her HbA1c is well below the usual default target. What is the most appropriate step in agreeing treatment targets with her?

options.text: Continue the current dose because a low HbA1c is always desirable
Agree a less stringent individual target and review whether the hypoglycaemia-causing medicine can be reduced or stopped
Increase the dose to move the HbA1c nearer the default target
Stop all treatment and discharge her from the diabetes register

questions.correctOptionText: Agree a less stringent individual target and review whether the hypoglycaemia-causing medicine can be reduced or stopped

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: very low values with hypoglycaemia in a frail patient represent over-treatment, not success.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: individualising the target and reducing harm is appropriate in frailty.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: increasing a hypoglycaemic drug would worsen the harm.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: she still has diabetes and needs review, foot and kidney checks; she should stay on the register.

questions.explanation: Targets are individualised to frailty, comorbidity and risk of harm. A frail older person with recurrent hypoglycaemia is over-treated, so the appropriate response is a relaxed target and de-intensifying the offending medicine while continuing structured review. Check current NICE guidance and local protocols before changing treatment.

questions.stem: A practice pharmacist performs a structured medication review for a patient taking many regular medicines. Which is the main aim of this review?

options.text: To replace all branded medicines with the cheapest alternative
To check with the patient that each medicine is still needed, effective, safe and actually being taken as intended
To assess whether the patient meets the criteria for QOF payment
To reduce the number of tablets regardless of the patient's conditions

questions.correctOptionText: To check with the patient that each medicine is still needed, effective, safe and actually being taken as intended

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: cost may be one factor but is not the main aim.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: structured medication review assesses need, effectiveness, safety and adherence with the patient.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: QOF is a practice-level incentive and not the purpose of an individual patient's review.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: reducing numbers is not the aim; deprescribing is by evidence and shared decision.

questions.explanation: Structured medication review is a patient-centred process: it explores what the patient takes, why, and whether it is still appropriate. It supports medicines optimisation by improving outcomes and reducing avoidable harm, not simply by cutting costs or tablet counts.

questions.stem: A man with hypertension reports that his clinic readings are often higher than his readings at home. What is the main reason to support him to monitor his blood pressure at home with a validated device?

options.text: It provides readings in his usual environment, helps to identify clinic-related elevation and engages him in his own care
It removes the need for any clinic review
Home readings are always higher than clinic readings and so give a safety margin
The readings can be used to adjust his medicine doses without any clinician review

questions.correctOptionText: It provides readings in his usual environment, helps to identify clinic-related elevation and engages him in his own care

distractorRationale.a: Correct: home monitoring gives out-of-clinic data and supports self-management.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: clinic review remains necessary for medicines, tests and risk assessment.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: home readings are typically lower than clinic readings, and have their own thresholds.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: dose changes should be made by a clinician using agreed protocols.

questions.explanation: Home blood pressure monitoring supports diagnosis and follow-up because it samples blood pressure away from the clinical setting and involves the patient in self-management. Because home values are typically lower than clinic values, home targets differ from clinic targets, and interpreting them still needs clinician input.

questions.stem: QOF indicators are practice-level incentives and should therefore be applied identically to every patient, whatever their frailty or preferences.
questions.explanation: QOF is a population-level scheme that rewards practices for achieving processes and outcomes, but individual care must still be tailored to the patient. Personalised care adjustment (exception reporting) exists because applying a target mechanically to a frail or informed-dissenting patient can cause harm.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes is given a laboratory report showing HbA1c 64 mmol/mol. Using HbA1c(%) = 0.0915 x HbA1c(mmol/mol) + 2.15, what is the equivalent DCCT value in per cent (%)? Give your answer to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Substituting gives 0.0915 x 64 = 5.856, and 5.856 + 2.15 = 8.006. This rounds to 8.0%, which is the older-style percentage equivalent of 64 mmol/mol.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma is prescribed one preventer inhaler canister per 28 days. Over a 168-day interval, the pharmacy record shows that 4 canisters were collected. Calculate the proportion of days covered, as a percentage, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Days' supply collected is 4 x 28 = 112 days. Dividing by the 168-day interval gives 112/168 = 0.667, or 66.7%. This suggests under-use of the preventer and should lead to a supportive discussion about barriers and technique, not an assumption of poor adherence.

questions.stem: Describe the content of a structured annual review for an adult with asthma, and explain how it supports self-management.
markingGuide: Recall system and register: invited at least annually, with additional review after an exacerbation or hospital attendance
Assess symptom control using a validated tool or direct questions on day and night symptoms and activity limitation
Record reliever use, exacerbations and oral steroid courses; overuse of reliever suggests poor control
Check inhaler technique and adherence to preventer; demonstrate and re-check
Ask about triggers and smoking and offer support
Review and update the written personalised action plan, and teach recognition of worsening and when to seek urgent help
questions.explanation: A strong answer links each element of the review to what the patient does between visits. The written action plan, inhaler technique teaching and discussion of reliever overuse make the review a self-management intervention and not just data collection.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old night-shift worker with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes asks 'what number do I have to hit?'. Explain how you would set an individual HbA1c target with him.
markingGuide: Explore his ideas, concerns and expectations, and what matters most to him (work, driving, family)
Explain the benefits of tighter control (reduced long-term complications) and the harms (hypoglycaemia risk with some drugs, treatment burden)
Consider his age, comorbidity, medicines prescribed and occupational risks such as driving or night work
Refer to the default NICE target while noting it is a starting point; check current guidance
Agree a specific target and timescale, document it, and plan a recheck
Agree how progress will be monitored and revisit the target as circumstances change
questions.explanation: Shared target setting balances benefit and harm for the person in front of you. The guideline default is the starting point, but the agreed number is individual, documented and reviewable.

questions.stem: A practice wants to improve long-term condition care for patients with multiple medicines and conditions. Compare the roles of the practice nurse, the practice pharmacist and the GP, and explain how the team supports medicines optimisation.
markingGuide: Practice nurse: structured review clinics, measurement, education, inhaler technique, protocol-led monitoring
Practice pharmacist: structured medication review, polypharmacy and deprescribing, reconciliation after discharge
GP: diagnosis, complexity and multimorbidity decisions, prescribing oversight, safety-netting
Medicines optimisation principles: understand patient experience, evidence-based choice, safety, routine practice
Adherence and shared decision making; communication between team members and clear documentation
Awareness that roles vary locally and that scope of practice is defined by competency and regulation
questions.explanation: A good answer recognises that the team members have overlapping but distinct roles and links them to the principles of medicines optimisation. Communication and clear documentation prevent duplication and errors.
